item.title: Pope Leo XIV’s planned lung surgery: What a lung nodule means, why it needs removal and what comes next
item.description: Pope Leo XIV is due to undergo surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital to remove a small, localised lung nodule detected during recent medical examinations. The Vatican expects about a week of recovery, but has not disclosed whether the growth is cancerous.
item.dc:creator: Trisha Bhattacharya
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo XIV is set to undergo surgery to remove a small nodule in his lung after doctors discovered the growth during recent medical examinations, prompting questions about the condition, the procedure and what it could mean for the pontiff’s health.Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgeryThe 71-year-old pope announced the planned operation during his Sunday Angelus address on 11 October, telling worshippers that the nodule had been detected at a very early stage and was well localised.He said his doctors had recommended surgery and that he had decided to follow their advice.According to Vatican News, Leo is scheduled to be admitted to Rome’s Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday, 13 October. The Vatican has estimated that his recovery will take approximately one week, with public engagements cancelled until 20 October.Despite the planned operation, the pope maintained his scheduled meetings on Monday, including engagements with bishops and members of a charitable organisation, Reuters reported.What is a lung nodule?A lung nodule is a small area of abnormal tissue in the lung, generally measuring up to 3 centimetres in diameter. Such growths can be discovered incidentally during scans conducted for other medical reasons, including investigations into infections or other health concerns.The finding does not automatically indicate cancer. Lung nodules can be benign, arising from causes such as previous infections or scar tissue, but some may be malignant.Their significance depends on factors including their size, appearance, location and changes over time.The Vatican has not disclosed whether Leo’s nodule is benign or cancerous, nor has it released detailed imaging results or a specific diagnosis.Why are doctors recommending surgery?The pope said his medical team considered an operation the appropriate course of action. Removing a nodule can allow doctors to examine the tissue and, depending on the diagnosis, may also treat the underlying condition.The exact surgical technique planned for Leo has not been publicly specified. Some lung nodules can be removed using minimally invasive procedures, although the appropriate approach depends on the individual case and the growth’s characteristics. Medical experts cited in coverage by the Associated Press have noted that when a cancerous lung nodule is identified and removed at an early stage, outcomes can be favourable. That general observation should not be taken as an indication that the pope has cancer.Will the surgery affect his papal duties?The Vatican has said the operation will require changes to Leo’s immediate schedule, with public engagements suspended during his expected recovery. The Holy See’s administration will continue to function while he is away from public duties.The pope is also scheduled to undertake an 11-day pastoral visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November. As of Monday, no changes to that trip had been announced.Leo, elected pope in May 2025, has continued his public engagements in the days leading up to the operation. His decision to disclose the medical finding has also provided a degree of transparency about his health, although important details remain private.

item.title: Trump’s Russia diesel deal sparks bipartisan backlash: Why the move is under fire
item.description: Trump’s move to ease sanctions on Russian diesel imports to curb soaring US fuel prices has triggered bipartisan backlash, raising questions over Washington’s efforts to pressure Moscow over the Ukraine war and whether the deal will offer meaningful relief to American consumers.
item.dc:creator: Bhanu Pratap
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel imports in an effort to bring down fuel prices has triggered bipartisan criticism, highlighting the tension between domestic economic pressures and Washington’s efforts to curb Moscow’s revenues from its war against Ukraine. Trump defended the move on Monday, arguing that European countries had continued to pay Russia substantial sums for energy. The announcement followed a conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin, after which Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to the US and global markets. The decision has drawn objections from lawmakers in both parties, who warn that relaxing restrictions could undermine efforts to pressure Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also criticised the arrangement, arguing that additional Russian energy revenues could help sustain the war. The controversy comes as US fuel prices surge amid disruptions linked to the war involving Iran, attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and tighter supplies of refined petroleum products. Why is Trump turning to Russian diesel? Trump announced the agreement on Friday after a discussion with Putin. Under the arrangement, Russia was expected to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, with further shipments anticipated in the following months. The move is intended to increase fuel availability at a time when rising diesel prices are putting pressure on the US economy amid inflation. Trump defended his decision in a post on Truth Social, writing: “The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story.”“I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he said in a post on Truth Social. The decision also comes ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3, when fuel costs and inflation could influence voters’ assessments of the administration’s economic performance. Fuel prices and inflation: Will the deal help Americans? The average US diesel price reached $6.28 per gallon on Thursday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), after rising about 70% since the US-Israeli war against Iran began on February 28. Higher diesel prices can feed into inflation by increasing costs for freight, food distribution, farming and manufacturing. Businesses may pass some of these expenses on to consumers, making fuel prices an economic concern that extends well beyond the transport sector. However, Reuters has reported questions about whether the Russian supplies would be sufficient to make a substantial difference to the market. An initial shipment of more than 300,000 tonnes would represent an addition to supply, but its impact would depend on delivery schedules, subsequent volumes and the extent of wider disruptions. The Trump administration is also considering measures to boost domestic fuel production. Reuters reported that officials were exploring ways to address restrictions affecting energy output and potentially invoke the Cold War-era Defence Production Act to support domestic oil and fuel supplies. Why are US lawmakers opposing the deal? The arrangement has drawn criticism from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who argue that easing restrictions on Russian fuel risks weakening Washington’s policy towards Moscow. A bipartisan group of senators urged Trump to reverse the decision, arguing that it could conflict with measures introduced after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. “Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's brutal war against Ukraine,” the lawmakers said in a statement, according to Reuters. Republican Senator Thom Tillis also questioned the legality of the arrangement, arguing that there was a case to be made that the president was not complying with the law. The criticism highlights the tension between the administration’s immediate objective of lowering domestic fuel prices and its longer-term strategy of restricting Russian revenues. What does the deal mean for sanctions on Russia? Western sanctions have sought to limit Russia’s access to revenue and international markets following its invasion of Ukraine. Easing restrictions on Russian diesel creates a potential contradiction in that strategy: Washington is seeking to increase fuel supplies while continuing to apply economic pressure on Russia over the war. A limited, temporary exemption would have a different impact from a sustained reopening of the US market to Russian petroleum products. The decision also raises questions about the consistency of US policy towards its allies. Washington has previously sought to limit countries’ purchases of Russian energy, including by threatening additional tariffs on India over its energy ties with Moscow. The diesel arrangement could therefore complicate Washington’s efforts to persuade other countries to restrict Russian energy purchases, particularly if the US itself relaxes restrictions to address domestic economic pressures. Ukraine warns Russia could benefit from the arrangement Zelenskyy has criticised the decision, arguing that allowing Russia to earn more from petroleum products could help finance its continued military campaign. The announcement came as Ukrainian and US officials were holding discussions on efforts to resolve the war. According to an Axios report, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the prospect of lifting sanctions on Russian diesel during talks with Ukrainian negotiators in Miami. The report also said Zelenskyy had offered to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian power plants. The conflict involving Iran has added pressure on global energy markets, with disruptions to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz—a critical route for international oil and petroleum product trade—contributing to concerns over supply and prices. The Russian diesel arrangement is therefore an attempt to address a supply problem with both geopolitical and logistical dimensions.
